newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai commercial banks seen raising lending rates.
newsitem.headline: Thai commercial banks seen raising lending rates.

text.p: An imminent, limited hike in Thai commercial lending rates is a cost that Thailand is likely to pay in its current battle to defend the baht from speculative attacks, analysts and bankers said on Thursday.

"I think rates are on an upward trend at the moment because of the money market. The key factor is baht speculation. While the weakening dollar may have eased things a little, I think it is only temporary," said the Thai Farmers Bank Research Center.
The baht has so far successfully weathered two major speculative assaults in six months.
The Bank of Thailand dollar/baht midrate was fixed at 25.98 on Thursday, down from 25.71 a month ago.

But the central bank's commitment to retaining its baht fixing practice requires high rates to attract foreign capital and maintain currency demand until an economic upturn lifts investor confidence, analysts said.
As part of its currency protection measures, the Bank of Thailand has made a commitment to absorb excess liquidity in the interbank money market.
The rising cost of borrowing from this market last week saw several smaller banks raise deposit rates to help mobilise more domestic deposits, analysts said.

Those rate rises may signal increasing competition for deposits, and comments by government economic advisor Olarn Chaipravat earlier this week asking firms to prepare for a prolonged bout of high rates, may signal a modest rate hike from the larger banks, analysts said.
The cost to the banks will be passed on in the form of higher lending rates, analysts said.
"I think we are likely to see a 25 basis point rise in prime rates soon," said an SBC Warburg analyst.

While the biggest lenders, including Bangkok Bank which controls some 25 percent of the country's deposits, have adopted a wait-and-see attitude to raising their rates, bank executives accept a small rise is now likely.

"I think we may see a small hike in rates to find out where market equilibrium is and then find that rates stay there for two to three months," said Wisit Wongpaisan, senior vice president of the Bank of Asia's treasury department.
"I think we are in a rising trend but it's not a trend where we have a rise in two weeks' time followed by two or three more over the next few months," Wisit said.
Adding to pressure to raise rates was the announcement last Friday that ratings agency Moody's Investors Service may downgrade Thailand's long term debt status, analysts said.

"A possible Moody's downgrade would raise (the) costs of raising offshore funds so the banks will look at increasing domestic deposits and the increasing competition will cause rates to rise," said the SBC Warburg analyst.
But a further rate hike would spell bad news for Thai corporates already struggling to cope with annual minimum domestic borrowing costs at some 13.25-14.25 percent, analysts said.
Sluggish corporate growth and tightening liquidity would mean lower overall economic growth which could be remedied by lowering interest rates.
But if rates were on an uptrend, Thailand could move further away from the upbeat economic outlook which would eventually allow rates to fall, analysts said.
"The banks really don't want to do this if at all possible because it means rising defaults and more non-performing loans. It's a no-win situation," said the SBC Warburg analyst.
